The Lord who, abiding within all, sees good and evil — to that Vishnu, witness of all, the supreme Lord, I bow.
vishnupurana:19:82	Salutation to that Vishnu from whom this world is not different; he is to be meditated on, the first of the worlds — may that imperishable one be gracious to me.
vishnupurana:19:83	He in whom this universe is woven warp and woof, called the imperishable, the support of all — may that Hari be gracious to me.
vishnupurana:19:84	Om, salutation to that Vishnu, salutation to him again and again, in whom is all, from whom is all, who is all and everywhere.
vishnupurana:19:85	Because the Infinite pervades all, I myself am he; all is from me, I am all, all is in me, the eternal.
vishnupurana:19:86	I alone am the imperishable, the eternal, the supreme self resting in the self; I am called Brahman at the beginning and likewise the Supreme Person at the end.
The great ocean, its hosts of crocodiles whirling, its waves surging, was agitated, and the whole earth shook with its mountains, woods and forests.
And the wise one, throwing off the mass of mountains placed on him by the daityas, came up out of that water.
Seeing the world again, marked by the sky and the rest, Prahlada by himself remembered himself again: "I am Prahlada."
And the wise one praised again the beginningless Supreme Person, with one-pointed mind, undistracted, restrained in speech, body and mind:
As he praised thus with his mind fixed on him, the god, the blessed Hari, clad in yellow garments, appeared.
Seeing him, he rose in agitation and, with faltering syllables, said again and again, "Salutation to Vishnu," brahmin:
God, remover of the distress of those who take refuge, be gracious, Keshava; purify me again by the gift of your glance, imperishable one.
I am pleased with you, who practise unswerving devotion; choose from me the boon you desire, Prahlada.

Lord, in whatever thousands of births I pass through, in each of them may my devotion to you be unfailing, Achyuta, always.
vishnupurana:20:19	Such unfailing love as the undiscerning have for sense objects, may it never leave my heart as I remember you.
You already have devotion to me, and it will be so again; choose from me whatever further boon you desire, Prahlada.

My father bore persistent hatred toward me because I was engaged in praising you; may the sin he thereby committed perish, god.
vishnupurana:20:22	The weapons struck on my body, my being thrown into the heap of fire, my being bitten by serpents, the poison put in my food,
vishnupurana:20:23	my being bound and thrown into the ocean and heaped over with rocks, and the other wrongs my father did me —
vishnupurana:20:24	the sin arising from hatred of one devoted to you — by your grace, lord, may my father be freed from it at once.
Prahlada, all this shall be yours by my grace. I give you yet another boon; choose it, son of the asura.

I have attained my purpose, Blessed One, by this boon, that by your grace I shall have unswerving devotion to you.
vishnupurana:20:27	What are dharma, wealth and desire to him? Liberation lies in the hand of him whose devotion is steadfast in you, the root of all worlds.
As your mind, full of devotion, is unwavering toward me, so by my grace you will attain supreme nirvana.
Having said this, Vishnu vanished while he watched, Maitreya; and he came back again and saluted his father's feet.
His father kissed him on the head and embraced him, who had suffered, and said, "You are alive, child!", his eyes wet with tears, brahmin.
The great asura grew affectionate toward him, repenting; and he, knowing dharma, likewise served his guru and his father.
When his father had been brought to his end by Vishnu in the form of the Man-Lion, he became lord of the daityas, Maitreya.
Having attained the glory of that kingdom, which purifies through action, brahmin, and many sons and grandsons and sovereignty,
when his authority was exhausted and he was free of merit and sin, he attained supreme nirvana through meditation on the Blessed One.
Such was the power of that daitya of great wisdom, Maitreya, Prahlada the devotee of the Blessed One, about whom you asked me.
Whoever hears this story of the great-souled Prahlada, his sins are at once destroyed.
A man who hears or recites the story of Prahlada, Maitreya, removes the sin committed in a day and a night, no doubt.
Reciting it on the full moon, the new moon, the eighth or the twelfth, brahmin, one obtains the fruit of giving a cow.

As Hari protected Prahlada in all calamities, so he protects whoever always hears his story. Compassionate to those who bow at his feet, fierce to those hostile to the humble — I salute the Man-Lion, giver of boons to Prahlada, terrible with his blazing radiance.
Vinata's two sons are renowned, Garuda and Aruna; Suparna, best of birds, is fierce and eats serpents.
Surasa's offspring were a thousand serpents of boundless might, many-headed, brahmin, great-souled sky-goers.
The sons of Kadru were a thousand mighty ones of boundless strength, brahmin, many-headed, subject to Suparna.
The chief among them are Shesha, Vasuki and Takshaka, Shankha, Shveta, Mahapadma, Kambala and Ashvatara,
Elaputra the naga, Karkotaka and Dhananjaya; these and many others, biting creatures fierce with poison.
Know the host born of Krodhavasha: all of them fanged, born on land, birds and water-born, fierce eaters of flesh; and from Krodha she produced the mighty pishachas.
Surabhi bore cows and buffaloes; Ira bore trees, creepers, vines and all kinds of grass.
Khasha bore yakshas and rakshasas, Muni the apsarases, and Arishta bore the gandharvas of great might.
These, the descendants of Kashyapa, moving and unmoving, have been told, and their sons and grandsons by the hundreds and thousands.
This creation is remembered as that of the Svarochisha Manvantara, brahmin. In the Vaivasvata, at the great and extensive sacrifice of Varuna,
the creation of offspring by Brahma as he offered is told here; where formerly the seven sages had arisen, seven mind-born ones,
the Grandsire himself appointed them as sons, best of beings, of the gandharvas, serpents, gods and danavas.
Diti, whose sons had been destroyed, propitiated Kashyapa; well worshipped by her, Kashyapa, best of ascetics,
offered her a boon, and she then chose as her boon a son of boundless might able to slay Indra.
The best of sages granted that boon to his wife, and having given it, the composed Kashyapa said to her:

Your son will slay Shakra if you carry the embryo for a hundred years. A pregnant woman, fair one, must not eat at twilight; she must never stand or eat at the foot of trees; you will carry it collected, very careful and pure.
Having said this to the lady, the sage Kashyapa departed, and she carried the embryo, observing purity properly.
Knowing that the embryo was for his own death, Maghavan, lord of the immortals, came to serve her out of humility.
The chastiser of Paka stayed there, seeking an opening in her; when a hundred years were nearly past, the self-possessed one saw his chance:
Diti went to bed without washing her feet and fell asleep. He entered her womb,
and the wielder of the thunderbolt cut the great embryo into seven; being split by the thunderbolt, it wept most terribly.
Do not weep (ma rodih), Shakra said to it again and again. The embryo became sevenfold, and Indra, angered again,
cut each one into seven with his foe-rending thunderbolt; they became the gods called the Maruts, exceedingly swift.
From what Maghavan said they became the Maruts, forty-nine gods, companions of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
The lords of beasts, the lords of birds, the rulers of men, of snakes and of nagas,
the rulers of trees, mountains and planets — past, present and those yet to be — all are born of portions of Vishnu, who is all beings.
For without Hari, lord of all, abiding in preservation, no one else has the power of protection, wise one.
The eternal one creates the world at creation, protects it in preservation, and destroys it as the ender, resorting to rajas, sattva and the rest.
Janardana is fourfold in creation, abides fourfold in preservation and brings about dissolution at the end in four divisions.
With one portion he becomes Brahma, possessing an unmanifest form; with another part the lords of creatures, Marichi and the rest;
Time is his third portion, and all beings another; thus, with rajas, he operates fourfold in creation.
Vishnu abiding with one portion carries out protection; with another in the form of Manu and the rest, with another as Time,
and with another abiding in all beings he maintains the world, the Supreme Person resorting to the guna of sattva.
Likewise at the time of the end the lord, resorting to the function of tamas, the unborn Blessed One becomes Rudra with one portion;
with another part he acts as fire, death and the rest; another part is of the form of Time, and another is all beings.
Thus for that great-souled one bringing destruction fourfold, the arrangement into divisions is told, brahmin, for all time.
Brahma, Daksha and the rest, Time and all creatures — these are the glories of Hari, causes of the world's creation.
Vishnu, Manu and the rest, Time and all beings, brahmin — these are the glories of Vishnu, the cause of preservation.
Rudra, Time, death and the rest, and all creatures — these are the fourfold glories of Janardana for dissolution.
At the beginning and in the middle of the world, creation is carried on until dissolution, brahmin, by the Creator, by Marichi and the rest and by the creatures.
Brahma creates at the first time; then Marichi and the others produce offspring, and creatures do so at every moment.
Without Time, brahmin, Brahma does not accomplish creation, nor do the Prajapatis, nor all creatures.
Just so this fourfold division of the god of gods is taught for preservation and likewise for dissolution, Maitreya.
Whatever is created by whatever kind of being, brahmin, in the origin of that created thing all of it is Hari's body.
Whatever being, unmoving or moving, anyone destroys anywhere, that is the fierce, ending body of Janardana, Maitreya.
Thus the god Janardana is the creator of the world, its protector, the world itself and the devourer of the whole world.
At the times of creation, preservation and end he operates thus threefold through the working of the gunas; his supreme state is great and without gunas.
That consists of knowledge, is all-pervading, known only to itself and incomparable; that form of the supreme self too is fourfold.
Tell me duly, sage, the fourfold nature of that which is Brahman, what is called the supreme state.
Maitreya, the cause is called the means in all things, and the end is the thing desired that one seeks to accomplish.
For the yogi desiring liberation, breath control and the rest are the means, and the end is the supreme Brahman, from which there is no return.
The knowledge that rests on the means, which the yogis have for liberation — that is the first division of him who is knowledge, sage.
The knowledge resting on the end, the Brahman to be attained by the yogi who practises for release from afflictions, is the second portion, great sage.
The non-dual knowledge in which end and means are undivided — that is the other part I have spoken of.
And that which is distinct from these three kinds of knowledge, great sage, like the nature of the self shown by the way of negating them,
without activity, indescribable, mere pervasion, incomparable, the object of self-realization, mere being, without marks,
utterly tranquil, fearless, pure, hard to conceive, without support — that knowledge is declared the supreme state of Vishnu who consists of knowledge.
The yogis who attain dissolution there through the cessation of ignorance become seedless in the field of worldly existence, brahmin.
Such is the supreme state called Vishnu — stainless, eternal, all-pervading, imperishable, free of everything to be rejected.
That is the supreme Brahman, from which the yogi does not return, when merit and demerit have ceased, his afflictions exhausted, utterly pure.
That Brahman has two forms, with form and formless; they are of the nature of the perishable and the imperishable and abide in all beings.

The imperishable is the supreme Brahman; the perishable is this whole world. As the moonlight of the moon, which stands in one place, spreads out, so this whole world is the power of the supreme Brahman.
And there, as the moonlight differs as more or less according to nearness or distance, so there is difference in his power, Maitreya.
Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, brahmin, are the chief powers of Brahman; below them, Maitreya, are the gods, and then Daksha and the rest;
then men, domestic beasts, wild beasts, birds and reptiles, less and still less, and then trees, bushes and the like.
This whole world, best of sages, is imperishable and eternal, yet subject to the alternatives of appearance and disappearance, birth and destruction.
Vishnu, consisting of all powers, is the other form of Brahman, the form with shape, on which yogis first meditate at the beginning of yoga.
The great yoga with a support, with a seed, in which he is established, arises, sage, for those who practise rightly with unobstructed mind.
He is supreme among all powers, next to Brahman; Brahman with form, fortunate one, is Hari, who consists of all Brahman.
In him all this whole world is woven warp and woof; from him is the world, the world is in him, and he is the whole world, sage.
Vishnu the Lord, consisting of the perishable and imperishable, bears all, consisting of spirit and unmanifest matter, in the form of ornaments and weapons.
This whole world which the blessed Vishnu bears in the form of ornaments and weapons — you should explain it to me.
Having bowed to the immeasurable, mighty Vishnu, I shall tell it as Vasishtha told it to me.
The blessed Hari bears the self of this world, untainted, without qualities and stainless, in the form of the Kaustubha gem — the pure spirit, knower of the field.
Pradhana is borne as the Shrivatsa mark, resting on the Infinite; intellect abides in Madhava in the form of the mace.
The Lord bears the twofold ego — the source of the elements and the source of the senses — in the form of the conch and of the Sharnga bow.
The mind, exceedingly restless, outstripping the wind in speed, he holds in the form of the discus abiding in Vishnu's hand.
The five-formed garland Vaijayanti of the mace-bearer is the aggregate of the causes of the elements, the garland of elements, brahmin.
All the senses, of perception and of action, Janardana bears in the form of arrows.
The most pure jewel of a sword that Achyuta bears is knowledge made of wisdom, set in the sheath of ignorance.
Thus spirit, pradhana, intellect and ego, the elements, the mind and all the senses, knowledge and ignorance, Maitreya — all this rests in Hrishikesha.
Though without form, Hari, in the form of maya, bears these in the shape of weapons and ornaments for the good of living beings.
Thus the lotus-eyed supreme Lord bears pradhana with its modifications, spirit and the whole world.
Whatever is knowledge and ignorance, whatever is existent and non-existent, Maitreya, all that is in the imperishable Madhusudana, lord of all beings.
With kala, kashtha, nimesha and the rest, days, seasons, half-years and years, the blessed Hari is of the form of Time, boundless and imperishable.
Bhurloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, best of sages, Mahar, Jana, Tapas and Satya — these seven worlds the all-pervading one
embodies as the self of the worlds; he is the elder even of the eldest; Hari himself abides as the support of all branches of knowledge.
In many forms — gods, men, beasts and the rest — the all-pervading, infinite lord of all abides, embodied as the elements yet formless.
The Rik, Yajus and Saman verses, and those of the Atharvan, the Itihasas and Upavedas, the statements of the Vedanta,
all the Vedangas, the laws declared by Manu and others, all the shastras, the stories and the anuvakas wherever they are,
whatever poetic utterances there are and all songs — this is the body of the great-souled Vishnu who bears the form of sound.
Whatever things there are, with form or formless, here or anywhere else, all of them are his body.
I am Hari; all this is Janardana; there is no collection of causes and effects other than him — one whose mind is thus is no longer afflicted by the diseases of the pairs born of existence.
Thus the first part of this Purana has been duly told to you, brahmin; by hearing it one is freed from sins.
Whatever fruit comes from bathing at Pushkara on the full moon of Kartika for twelve years, a man obtains all that by hearing this, Maitreya.
And the origins of gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakshas and the rest — for the man who hears them, the gods and the others become givers of boons, sage.
Whatever sin one commits by day is released by seeing it at night; and one lives as many years and more as there are stars resting on the Shishumara in the sky.
Uttanapada is to be known as its upper jaw, Yajna as its lower, and Dharma rests on its head;
Narayana is in its heart, the Ashvins in its forefeet, Varuna and Aryaman in its hind thighs;
the Year is its genitals, and Mitra occupies its anus.
In its tail are Agni, Mahendra, Kashyapa and then Dhruva; these four stars of the Shishumara never set.
Thus has been described the arrangement of the earth and the luminaries, of the continents, oceans and mountains,
of the regions and rivers and of those who dwell in them; their nature has been told; hear briefly again.
The water is Vishnu's body; from it, brahmin, arose the earth in the shape of a lotus, with its mountains, seas and the rest.
The luminaries are Vishnu, the worlds are Vishnu, the forests are Vishnu, the mountains and the quarters; the rivers and oceans are he; he is all that is and all that is not, best of brahmins.
Since the Blessed One is of the nature of knowledge, of all forms and not a mere thing, know the distinctions of mountains, oceans, earth and the rest to be the unfolding of consciousness.
But when, on the exhaustion of karma, all knowledge is pure, in its own form, free of faults, then there are no fruits of the tree of imagination, no distinctions of things among things.
Is there anything anywhere without beginning, middle and end, ever of one form? What becomes otherwise again, brahmin, is not truly so — how then is it reality?

Earth becomes a pot, the pot potsherds, the potsherds powdered dust, and that atoms; it is perceived by people whose certainty of self is dulled by their own karma. Tell me, what here is the real thing?

Therefore, brahmin, there is no collection of things anywhere, at any time, apart from consciousness; the one consciousness is taken as manifold by those whose minds are divided by the differences of their own karma.
Knowledge pure, stainless, free of sorrow, free of all attachment to greed and the rest, one, ever one, the supreme, the highest lord — he is Vasudeva, apart from whom nothing exists.
This true being I have told you: knowledge is the truth, everything else is untrue; but what belongs to ordinary dealing, that too, dwelling in the worlds, has been told you.

Sacrifice, the victim, the fire, all the priests, soma, the gods, and desire consisting of heaven — such is the path seen as resting on works, and the enjoyments of Bhur and the other worlds are their fruits.
And what I have told you about the worlds, one goes everywhere there subject to karma; knowing thus, one should seek that which is fixed, immovable and ever of one form, by which one enters Vasudeva.

Tell me, O king, what you have directly seen in me; 'strong' or 'weak' should be spoken afterwards as a qualification.
vishnupurana:35:61	'The palanquin is carried by you' and 'it rests on you even now' — this is false here; hear my words, sir.
vishnupurana:35:62	The pair of feet rests on the ground; the shanks stand on the two feet; the thighs rest on the two shanks, and the belly rests on them;
vishnupurana:35:63	the chest, the arms and the shoulders rest on the belly; this palanquin rests on the shoulders — how is the burden here mine?
vishnupurana:35:64	And this body seated in the palanquin, designated as you — there you are 'you' and I am here 'I'; this is said otherwise.
vishnupurana:35:65	I, you and others, lord of the earth, are borne by the elements; this host of elements too, fallen into the current of the gunas, moves along.
vishnupurana:35:66	These gunas, sattva and the rest, are subject to karma, lord of the earth; and karma is accumulated through ignorance in all creatures.
vishnupurana:35:67	The self is pure, imperishable, tranquil, without gunas, beyond prakriti; it has no growth or decline, being one in all creatures.
vishnupurana:35:68	When it has neither growth nor decline, O king, by what reasoning did you say 'You are stout'?
vishnupurana:35:69	If this palanquin rests on the shoulders, which rest on the earth, feet, shanks, hips, thighs, belly and the rest, then the burden is equal for you.
vishnupurana:35:70	Likewise, O king, by other creatures is borne not only the burden arising from the palanquin, but also that of mountains, trees and houses, and whatever arises from the earth.
vishnupurana:35:71	When the spirit is separate from the causes that are of prakriti, O king, which burden then is to be carried by me, lord of men?
vishnupurana:35:72	Of whatever substance this palanquin is made, of that substance is the aggregate of elements, yours, mine and of all this, magnified by the sense of 'mine'.
Having said this, the brahmin fell silent, carrying the palanquin; and the king too descended to the ground and hastily grasped his feet:

O, O, set down the palanquin and be gracious to me, brahmin; tell me who you are, standing here in the guise of a fool.
vishnupurana:35:75	Who you are, for what purpose, and what is the reason for your coming — tell me all this, learned one, for I wish to hear.

Hear: 'Who am I?' — this cannot be told, O king; and coming anywhere is for the sake of experience.
vishnupurana:35:77	Pleasure and pain are to be experienced, and they produce the body and the rest; to experience them, born of dharma and adharma, a creature takes on a body and the rest.
vishnupurana:35:78	For every creature everywhere, O king, dharma and adharma are the cause; so why ask the cause?

Dharma and adharma are without doubt the cause in all effects, and the embodied one's coming to another place is for the sake of experience.
vishnupurana:35:80	But what you said, that 'Who am I?' about oneself cannot be told — I wish to hear that.
vishnupurana:35:81	'He who exists is I' — how can this not be told, brahmin? The word 'I' applied to the self is no fault, brahmin.

The word 'I' is at fault, not the self; so it is. The knowledge of self in what is not the self, or the word, is the mark of error.
vishnupurana:35:83	The tongue says 'I', and the teeth, lips and palate, O king; none of these is 'I', since all are causes of producing speech.
vishnupurana:35:84	Does speech itself say 'I' by means of its causes? Even so, speech is not 'I'; to say this is not proper.
vishnupurana:35:85	Since the body marked by head, hands and the rest is separate from the spirit, where, O king, should I apply this name 'I'?
vishnupurana:35:86	If there were some other being distinct from me, best of kings, then one might say 'This is I, and that is another.'
vishnupurana:35:87	But when one spirit abides in all bodies, then 'Who are you? Who am I?' is a fruitless speech.
vishnupurana:35:88	'You are the king, this is the palanquin, we are the bearers in front, and this is your people' — this is not true, O king.
vishnupurana:35:89	From the tree comes wood, and from that this palanquin on which you sit; where has the name 'tree' or the name 'wood' gone, O king?
vishnupurana:35:90	These people do not say of you 'The great king is mounted on a tree,' nor does anyone say you are on wood; they say you are in a palanquin.
vishnupurana:35:91	The palanquin is an aggregate of wood standing in an arrangement; search for the palanquin, best of kings, when it is taken apart.
vishnupurana:35:92	Likewise consider the separateness of the ribs of an umbrella — where has the umbrella gone? The same reasoning applies to you and to me.
vishnupurana:35:93	'Man, woman, cow, horse, elephant, bird, tree' — these worldly names applied to bodies are to be understood as caused by karma.
vishnupurana:35:94	The spirit is neither god nor man nor beast nor tree; these differences of bodily shape, O king, are births caused by karma.
vishnupurana:35:95	What in the world is called 'king', what consists of the king's soldiers, and anything else, O king — that is not real, but made of imagination.
vishnupurana:35:96	That which even after a lapse of time does not take on another name, arising from transformation and the like, is the real thing, O king — and what is that?
vishnupurana:35:97	You are king to all the people, son to your father, enemy to your enemy, husband to your wife, father to your son — as what shall I speak of you, O king?
vishnupurana:35:98	Are you this head, or is the head yours, and likewise the belly? Are you the feet and so on, or are these yours, lord of the earth?
vishnupurana:35:99	You stand apart from all your limbs, O king; become skilled and reflect, 'Who am I?'
vishnupurana:35:100	When reality is thus established, how can I say 'I', which is produced only by separating out, O king?

I do not carry the palanquin, nor does the palanquin rest on me; the body by which this palanquin is borne is other than me.
vishnupurana:36:5	The activity of beings, impelled by karma, is through the working of the gunas; and these gunas act — why did you say 'mine'?

Knower of the highest truth, when this reached my ears, my mind became distraught, having turned to seek the highest truth.
vishnupurana:36:7	Earlier, brahmin, I had set out to go and ask the fortunate sage Kapila, without doubt, 'What indeed is the highest good?'
vishnupurana:36:8	Meanwhile, by these words you have spoken, my mind runs to you for the sake of the highest truth.
vishnupurana:36:9	The sage Kapila, they say, is a portion of the blessed Vishnu, who is all beings, come to earth to destroy the delusion of the world.
vishnupurana:36:10	Surely that same Blessed One, out of desire for our good, has become manifest here, as this is spoken by you.
vishnupurana:36:11	So tell me, who bow to you, what is the highest good, brahmin; you are an ocean with waves of the waters of all knowledge.

O king, do you ask what is good, or do you ask the highest truth? All good things are other than the highest truth, lord of the earth.
vishnupurana:36:13	Having worshipped the gods, one desires riches, one desires sons and kingship; the good is marked by attaining these.
vishnupurana:36:14	Ritual action consisting of sacrifice is a good that gives the fruit of heaven; the chief good is that same action when its fruit is not sought.
vishnupurana:36:15	The self is always to be meditated on by those joined in yoga, O king, and likewise the Supreme; the good is the union of the self with the supreme self.
vishnupurana:36:16	Thus there are many goods, by the hundreds and thousands, but these are not the highest truth; hear me.
vishnupurana:36:17	If wealth were the highest truth, why is it given up for dharma, and why is it spent, being marked by the attainment of desires?
vishnupurana:36:18	If a son is called the highest truth, lord of men, he too is the highest truth for another, and his father is the highest truth for another.
vishnupurana:36:19	Thus there is no highest truth in this world of moving and unmoving, for effects become causes endlessly.
vishnupurana:36:20	If the attainment of kingship and the like is called the highest truth here, then they are highest truths at one time and not at another.
vishnupurana:36:21	If you consider sacrificial action accomplished by the Rik, Yajus and Saman to be the highest truth, hear what I say about that too.
vishnupurana:36:22	Whatever effect is produced from clay as its cause is known to be made of clay, O king, because it follows its cause.
vishnupurana:36:23	Thus the rite which is produced by perishable substances, fuel, ghee, kusha and the like, will itself be perishable.
vishnupurana:36:24	The highest truth is accepted by the wise as imperishable; but that is perishable without doubt, being produced from perishable substances.
vishnupurana:36:25	If you think that action performed without seeking fruit is the highest truth, being a means to liberation — a means is not the highest truth.
vishnupurana:36:26	And meditation on the self, O king, spoken of as for the sake of the highest truth, creates a distinction from others; the highest truth has no distinction.
vishnupurana:36:27	The union of the self with the supreme self is held to be the highest truth; this is false, for one substance does not become another substance.
vishnupurana:36:28	Therefore all these are goods, O king, no doubt; but hear from me briefly the highest truth, lord of the earth.
vishnupurana:36:29	The self is one, all-pervading, equal, pure, without gunas, beyond prakriti, free of birth, growth and the rest, omnipresent and imperishable,
vishnupurana:36:30	consisting of supreme knowledge, the lord, not joined with unreal names, classes and the like; it was not joined, is not joined and will not be joined, lord of the earth.
vishnupurana:36:31	The knowledge that it is of one nature in one's own and others' bodies — that is the highest truth; the dualists do not see reality.
vishnupurana:36:32	As the one undivided, all-pervading air gets distinctions named shadja and the rest through the different holes of a flute, so with that great-souled one:
vishnupurana:36:33	his oneness appears as differences of form arising from the operation of outer actions; when the distinctions of god and the rest are destroyed, there is no veil at all.
Where do you dwell, brahmin, where are you setting out to go, and from where have you come? Tell me that, brahmin.

He who has hunger gets satisfaction when food is eaten, brahmin; I had no hunger — why do you ask me about satisfaction?
vishnupurana:37:20	When the earthy element is consumed by fire, hunger arises; and when the water is depleted, thirst too arises in men.
vishnupurana:37:21	Hunger and thirst are called properties of the body, and since they are not mine, brahmin, and hunger does not arise, I am always satisfied.
vishnupurana:37:22	Ease of mind and contentment are properties of the mind, brahmin; ask him whose mind it is — the spirit is not joined with these.
vishnupurana:37:23	As for your asking 'Where do you dwell?', 'Where will you go?' and 'From where do you come?' — learn from me about all three.
vishnupurana:37:24	Since the spirit is omnipresent and all-pervading like space, how can 'from where', 'where' and 'where will you go' have meaning?
vishnupurana:37:25	I neither go nor come, nor dwell in one place; neither you nor others are you or others, nor am I I.
vishnupurana:37:26	'Sweet or not sweet' — this inquiry of mine was made to see what you would say; hear about that too, best of the twice-born.
vishnupurana:37:27	What is unsavoury or sweet to one eating food, best of the twice-born? The very sweet, when it becomes unsweet, is a cause of disgust.
vishnupurana:37:28	The unsweet becomes sweet, and people are disgusted with the sweet; at beginning, middle and end, what food gives pleasure?
vishnupurana:37:29	As a house made of clay, plastered with clay, becomes firm, so this earthy body is strengthened by earthy atoms; what enjoyment then does the spirit have here?
vishnupurana:37:30	Barley, wheat, mung beans and the rest, ghee, oil, milk, curd, jaggery, fruits and the like are all earthy atoms.
vishnupurana:37:31	Knowing this, you should make your mind, which judges sweet and unsweet, rest in equality, for equality leads to liberation.
Hearing his words based on the highest truth, O king, the fortunate Nidagha bowed and said:
Be gracious; for my good, tell me who you are who have come; my delusion is destroyed on hearing these words of yours, brahmin.

I am Ribhu, your teacher, come here to give you wisdom, brahmin; I shall go now; the highest truth has been told you.
vishnupurana:37:35	Know this whole world thus to be one, undivided, the nature of the supreme self called Vasudeva.
Nidagha said "So be it" and bowed; worshipped with supreme devotion, Ribhu departed as he wished.
Having said this, the learned guru Ribhu left Nidagha; and Nidagha too, by that teaching, became devoted to non-duality.
He then saw all beings as not different from himself, and likewise Brahman; then the brahmin attained supreme liberation.
So you too, knower of dharma, knowing the self to be all-pervading, be equal toward yourself, enemy and kinsman, lord of the earth.
As the one sky is seen as different by the distinctions of white, blue and the rest, so the self, though one, appears separate to those of deluded vision.
Whatever is here is the One, Achyuta; there is nothing beyond him or other than him. He is I, he is you, he is all this, the nature of the self; give up the delusion of difference."

Thus addressed by him, that best of kings gave up difference, seeing the highest truth; and he too, having gained awakening through remembrance of his former birth, attained final release in that very birth.

Whoever tells this essential story of King Bharata, and whoever hears it with devotion, becomes pure in mind, does not fall into self-delusion, and becomes fit for liberation in his wanderings through existence.

He will offer us on the earth, bowed with devotion, handfuls of water mixed with seven or eight grains of sesame.
vishnupurana:52:28	Having obtained it from somewhere, or a day's fodder for cows, in the absence of other things he will give it with faith, pleasing us.
vishnupurana:52:29	In the absence of everything, going to the forest and showing his armpits, he will recite this aloud to the Sun and the other world-guardians:
vishnupurana:52:30	'I have no wealth, no riches, nor anything else fit for shraddha; I bow to my ancestors. May the ancestors be satisfied by my devotion; I have raised these two arms in the path of the wind.'
This, sung by the ancestors, is the provision for having and not having; whoever does this has performed shraddha, lord of the earth.
Having recited the mantra that slays demons and strewn the ground with sesame, one should meditate on one's own ancestors as being those very best of brahmins:

May my father, grandfather and great-grandfather, dwelling in the bodies of the brahmins, attain satisfaction today.
vishnupurana:53:33	May my father, grandfather and great-grandfather, their forms nourished by the fire offering, attain satisfaction.
vishnupurana:53:34	May my father, grandfather and great-grandfather attain satisfaction by the pinda given by me on the ground.
vishnupurana:53:35	May my father, grandfather and great-grandfather attain satisfaction by my devotion in what I have brought here.
vishnupurana:53:36	May my maternal grandfather attain satisfaction, and likewise his father and the other; may the Vishvedevas attain supreme satisfaction, and may the yatudhanas perish.
vishnupurana:53:37	The lord of sacrifice, the imperishable Hari, enjoyer of all offerings to gods and ancestors, is the Lord here; by his presence may all rakshasas and all asuras depart at once.
When they are satisfied, one should scatter food on the ground before the brahmins and give them water once and again for rinsing the mouth.
Permitted by them when well satisfied, one should then, collected, properly offer pindas on the ground with all the food mixed with sesame.

With the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors one should give water, a handful of water; and with that same part offer pindas to the maternal grandfathers. One should carefully prepare a place sloping to the south, in clean open spaces and on the banks of waters.
On darbha grass with tips pointing south, honoured with flowers, incense and the like, one should offer the first pinda to one's father near the remnants,
another to the grandfather and another to his father; one should please those who partake of the residue by rubbing the residue at the root of the darbha.
Likewise with pindas furnished with sandal, garlands and the like one should honour the maternal grandfathers, and then give water for rinsing to the chief brahmins,
first to those representing the ancestors, with devotion and attention, lord of men, and give a fee according to means, with the blessing "susvadha."
Having given them the fee, one should have those representing the Vishvedevas say it, and say, "May the Vishvedevas be pleased."
When those brahmins have said "So be it," blessings should be requested; afterwards one should dismiss the ancestors first and then the gods, wise one.
The same order with the gods is prescribed for the maternal grandfathers, in feeding, in giving according to one's means and in dismissal.
From the washing of the feet onward, one should first attend to the brahmins representing the gods, but the dismissal of those representing the ancestors and maternal grandfathers comes first.
One should dismiss them, honoured with kind words and respect; permitted, one should turn back, having followed them to the door.
Then the wise man should perform the daily rite called Vaishvadeva, and eat together with those to be honoured, his servants and his kin.
Thus the wise man should perform shraddha for the paternal and maternal ancestors; nourished by shraddhas, the forefathers grant all desires.
Three things purify at shraddha: a daughter's son, the kutapa hour and sesame; likewise the gift of silver, and telling and showing it.
To be avoided by one performing shraddha are anger, travel and haste; for the one who eats as well, king of kings, these three are not commended.
The Vishvedevas, the ancestors and the maternal grandfathers, O king, and the whole family are nourished by men who perform shraddha.
The host of ancestors rests on the Moon, and the Moon rests on yoga; therefore the engagement of a yogi at shraddha is commended, lord of the earth.
If among even a thousand brahmins a yogi stands in front, he carries across all the eaters and the sacrificer too, O king.
Prasatika, nivara and the two kinds of shyamaka millet, and chiefly the wild grains, are fit for shraddha, bull among men.
Barley, priyangu, mung, wheat, rice, sesame, nishpava, kovidara and mustard are good here.
Any grain of which the first-fruits offering has not been made, lord of men, and rajamasha, anu and lentils should be avoided.
Gourd, carrot, onion, pindamulaka, gandharaka, karambha, salts and saline earth,
reddish exudations and visible salts — these are to be avoided at shraddha, and whatever is not commended by speech.
Water brought at night, not offered, in which a cow would not be satisfied, foul-smelling or frothy, is not fit for shraddha, lord of the earth.
The milk of one-hoofed animals, of camels and sheep, of deer and of buffaloes should be avoided in the shraddha rite.
If it is seen by eunuchs, outcasts, chandalas, heretics, madmen and the sick, by cocks, dogs, naked ascetics, monkeys and village pigs,
by women in their courses, women after childbirth, the impure and carriers of the dead, then at that shraddha neither gods nor ancestors eat, bull among men.
Therefore one should perform shraddha with faith in an enclosed place, and ward off the yatudhanas by scattering sesame on the ground.
Food should not be putrid, nor contaminated by hairs, insects and the like, O king, nor mixed with fermented liquids, nor stale.
What is given with faith to the ancestors by name and lineage, whatever food they have come to take, it becomes that food for them.
Verses sung by the ancestors are also heard, lord of the earth, long ago in the Kalapa grove of Ikshvaku, son of Manu:

Will there be in our family those who follow the good path, who will go to Gaya and offer us pindas with reverence?
vishnupurana:54:19	May one be born in our family who would give us on the thirteenth milk-rice with honey and ghee, in the rains and under Magha,
vishnupurana:54:20	or marry a maiden of eight, or release a dark bull, or sacrifice with the horse sacrifice according to rule with fees.
The words we shall speak for the worship of the worlds and of Vishnu the Lord — by them may the first, blessed Vishnu be gracious.
